images.alt:
Who will be the Most Improved Player of the Year?

Jones: Ausar Thompson. This could feel like a long shot considering there's a world where already good players (Brandon Miller, Dylan Harper) take another leap and get that level of recognition. With Thompson, it appears the Pistons have bet on him taking a stronger leap offensively by working to get the ball in his hands and moving him around the court. If he continues to showcase confidence to get to his spots and attack off the bounce, the math on the Pistons could change. Also the defense. All of the defense. 

Iko: Brandon Miller. With LaMelo Ball and Miles Bridges gone, head coach Charles Lee can fully shift principles towards Kon Knueppel and Miller — with the latter as my bet to take home this award. The runway is there for an uptick in playmaking and overall offensive usage, combined with some sneaky defensive chops and rim protection as a 6-foot-9 combo-ish wing. There's some work to do regarding some of the types of shots he takes — he has a propensity to force things up when he's compromised — but Lee is one of the brightest young minds around and should assist in that.

Haberstroh: Davion Mitchell. He slimmed down a ton in the offseason and looks like someone who's going to thrive next to Giannis Antetokounmpo in Erik Spoelstra's demanding uptempo system. Like NAW before him, Mitchell will shed his defensive specialist reputation and become a two-way force.

Devine: Jaden McDaniels. Now, will he actually be notably and demonstrably better than he's been in recent seasons, where he's ticked up his scoring, shooting efficiency and complementary playmaking while consistently performing like an All-Defensive Teamer on the wing? Or will running alongside LaMelo Ball just get him the extra couple of buckets per game that make him a 20-plus-point scorer, which in turn makes everybody look a little closer at those year-over-year improvements? If it results in a trophy … who cares, I guess, right?

Most Disappointing Team of the First Month …
Devine: Toronto Raptors. It's not a shock to me that they are 5-10, given the myriad injuries they've suffered — most notably, obviously, getting just two games out of Kawhi Leonard before he went down with amorphous, ill-defined knee woes that, in a recent report by the great Michael Grange of Sportsnet, evoked the phrase "mystery condition." (Who could have foreseen this?!?) I do find it disappointing, though, that a team that won 46 games with the point differential of a 50-win squad and a top-seven defense last season — without Leonard — has so often looked so feckless this season … and that it's a combined 0-8 against teams with .500 or better records, getting blitzed by 11.5 points per 100 possessions against opponents with top-10 net ratings. Maybe, with better health, the Raptors will turn things around. Right now, though, even given the absence of their big-ticket offseason acquisition, they seem disappointingly unserious.

items.body_excerpt: Remember when James Harden said that he's not a system player; he *is* the system? That's Karl-Anthony Towns right now in New York — the embodiment, exemplification and best expression of exactly how the Knicks want to play, and what makes the defending champs so dangerous: tinyurl.com/49zy86nx

images.alt:
Much of this stellar start goes back to those five principles — pace, space, quick decisions, paint touches, crash the glass — that Brown's been hammering ever since he got to New York. Towns might not be the first person you think of when you hear the word "pace," and the Knicks probably wouldn't be the first team to come to mind: They rank dead last in the NBA in number of possessions per 48 minutes, and tied for 28th in the average length of their offensive possessions. (Much, at times, to Brown's chagrin.) But while nobody will confuse Brown's charges for the Seven Seconds or Less Suns, they do move more swiftly with the 7-footer involved: The Knicks' average offensive possession is 1.3 seconds faster with Towns on the floor than off it — the largest differential of any Knick who's played actual minutes.

"Space," obviously, is a little easier to square here. Long heralded as perhaps the sweetest-shooting big man of all time (including, um, by himself), Towns is attempting eight 3-pointers per 100 possessions this season, the most since his last season in Minnesota and the fourth-most of his career. He boasts the third-highest average gravity of any center — an NBA Advanced Stats metric aiming to quantify "how much a player pulls defenders towards them [...] how much attention they draw compared to what the spacing on the floor predicts" — behind only Wembanyama and Joel Embiid. (Towns also outpaces both in perimeter gravity when he's off the ball, meaning he's drawing more attention than either of them when he's spaced and doesn't have possession — creating wider driving and passing lanes for his teammates to exploit.)

When Towns does have the ball, he's wasting precious little time before attacking. Among 80 players averaging at least 50 touches per game this season, Towns averages the second-fewest dribbles per touch and has the seventh-lowest average touch time, holding on to the ball for just 1.8 seconds on average, according to Second Spectrum tracking data. He's one of 12 Knicks under two seconds per touch — evidence of widespread adherence to Brown's insistence on quick decision-making.

When the big fella decides to move, he's often aimed at the lane. Despite spending a significant share of his floor time setting high ball screens, spacing the floor or facilitating from up top, Towns leads the Knicks in paint touches per game — he's 26th in the league in total paint touches — and is taking a career-high 53% of his shots at the rim this season.

He's actually driving to the cup less frequently — just 5.5 dribble-drives per game this season, down from 8.1 last season and 11.3 in 2024-25. He's been an absolute monster on those forays to the basket, though, scoring nearly a point per drive and shooting 67% on those plays. He's finishing tough through the contact he draws in the lane, too: Nearly 35% of the shooting fouls he absorbs have ended in an and-one — also near a career-high.

Thanks partly to the pressure Towns puts on the rim himself, and partly to how his presence on the perimeter opens up the floor for his teammates, the Knicks take 34.5% of their field-goal attempts at the rim with him in the game — a near-top-five rate in the league, according to Cleaning the Glass. That rate drops to 25.8% when he's off the floor, which would sit just 26th in the NBA.

That just leaves "crash the glass" … which Towns is doing to the tune of hauling in a career-high 11.3% of available offensive rebounds. He's turning the garbage into gold, too, tied for sixth in the NBA in second-chance points per game — one big reason why New York's in the top five in putback scoring efficiency.

items.body_excerpt: I'm not qualified to do much in this world. But I *am* uniquely suited to recognize when someone's using too many words to either say nothing or try NOT to say something. tinyurl.com/2vvh7ejk

images.alt:
That's a long way from where the Cavs — one of the most expensive rosters in the sport — want to be … and, from the sound of things, they've got some pretty big questions to answer before they can get there. From Danny Cunningham of The Inside Shot:

Donovan Mitchell, who had a game-high 28 points, was asked about the effort being inconsistent from quarter-to-quarter or game-to-game this season.

Mitchell thought for a full five seconds after the question was asked.

"I think," he said before pausing for eight more seconds. "I'm trying to figure out how not to end up on ESPN."

Mitchell continued.

"I think the biggest thing now is just figuring each other out. We're not here in the locker room panicking, and all I can say to that, is what we got going forward. Nights like tonight are bad. It's a bad night, and we got to respond to that. We've got to respond to that and just keep playing our game. There's so many different things you can point to, but at the end of the day for us, it's within us. I have all the confidence in everybody in here, and we've got all the confidence in each other. We've got to go out there and execute it. That doesn't really answer your question, but yeah."

If there's one thing I'm qualified to assess as a longtime professional blogger, it's this: That was a lot of words to not really make any point or address the issue at hand. Which, come to think of it, might constitute a pretty loud statement about the state of affairs in Cleveland right about now.
